title: FBR POS for Pharmacies in Pakistan: Compliance Without the Headaches
metaDescription: An FBR POS guide for Pakistani pharmacies in 2026 — batch and expiry tracking, DRAP alongside FBR, controlled items, and the IRIS settings that keep you compliant.
content:
Why pharmacy FBR compliance is its own challenge

An FBR POS system for a pharmacy reports every sale to the Federal Board of Revenue in real time while also handling the things only pharmacies deal with: hundreds of SKUs, batch and expiry tracking, mixed tax treatment across medicines, and DRAP obligations running in parallel. The FBR side is mandatory for Tier-1 retailers, but it has to coexist with all of that without slowing the counter.

The most common failure is not dramatic — it is a pharmacy that believes it is compliant while a chunk of its invoices quietly never reach FBR IRIS, surfacing only when a penalty notice arrives.

FBR and DRAP are separate — your POS should handle both

FBR cares that the sale and tax are reported; DRAP cares about batches, expiry, and controlled items. A capable pharmacy POS tracks batch and expiry for stock and DRAP while sending a clean, QR-coded invoice to IRIS for every sale. Treating one as a substitute for the other is a mistake.

Getting tax mapping right

This is where pharmacies trip up most. Medicines are not uniformly taxed — some are exempt, some carry specific rates. If the POS applies a flat rate to everything, patients are over-charged and FBR submissions are wrong, which invites an audit. Map each product to its correct treatment during setup and review it whenever rates change.

A practical setup sequence

  1. Verify your STRN is active on IRIS.
  2. Import your catalogue with correct tax categories per product.
  3. Enable batch and expiry tracking for stock and DRAP, separate from tax logic.
  4. Test invoices across exempt, standard, and specific-rate items and confirm each in IRIS.
  5. Set up offline queueing so billing never stops during an outage.
  6. Schedule a monthly reconciliation against the IRIS dashboard.

A real example: a Karachi medical store

A medical store in Karachi mapped every product to the standard rate to "keep it simple." Exempt medicines were taxed for two months before a customer complaint surfaced it. Beyond refunds, the wrong submissions had to be corrected with FBR. Re-mapping the catalogue and adding a monthly check ended the problem.

Staying compliant

Reconcile monthly, keep tax mapping current, and treat the IRIS dashboard — not the printed receipt — as proof a sale was reported. If submissions start failing, our guide to common FBR POS issues and fixes covers token expiry, offline sync, and QR validation, and the IRIS registration guide helps if you are still setting up.

faqs.question: Does an FBR POS replace my DRAP record-keeping?
faqs.answer: No. FBR compliance and DRAP requirements are separate. A good pharmacy POS helps with both — reporting sales to FBR IRIS while also tracking batches and expiry for DRAP — but neither obligation removes the other.

faqs.question: How does batch and expiry tracking interact with FBR invoicing?
faqs.answer: Batch and expiry tracking is for stock and DRAP, while the FBR invoice reports the sale and tax. They live in the same POS but serve different rules; the invoice still has to reach IRIS regardless of how stock is tracked.

faqs.question: Are all medicines taxed the same way on an FBR invoice?
faqs.answer: No — many medicines fall under specific or exempt categories. Mapping each product to the correct tax treatment is essential; applying a standard rate to exempt items over-charges patients and produces wrong FBR submissions.

faqs.question: What is the penalty risk for a small pharmacy?
faqs.answer: Even small pharmacies that are Tier-1 retailers face penalties starting around PKR 10,000 and rising for repeat non-compliance, plus possible STRN suspension. Silent submission failures are the usual cause.
